parts.text: Both Tolkien and Jansson’s respective imaginations were fundamentally shaped by Finnish myth and folklore. Moreover, Tolkien

borrowed from what he called the “linguistic aesthetics” of Finnish for his invented Elvish language Quenya.

Even bearing this in mind, Jansson’s black-and-white illustrations are very clearly a product of a world before Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings

(2001-2003) set the benchmark for visual adaptations of Tolkien’s work.

From Moominvalley to Middle-earth

In 1962, fantasy had not yet solidified as a distinct publishing genre. It would take the

of The Lord of the Rings into a full-blown cultural phenomenon in the late 1960s to do that. This gave artists greater license to interpret The Hobbit as a standalone work of children’s literature, rather than as a prequel to an epic

.

Jansson did not take The Hobbit’s intended audience as an excuse to “soften” her visualisation of Middle-earth, however. In a 1961 essay, she opined that there is an “intense horror sensation […] in every honest children’s book”. As

of children’s literature Olga Holownia has explained: “An opportunity to create horror-infused landscapes was Jansson’s key motivation behind taking on the Tolkien commission. She found the scenery ‘seductive in its macabre

’.”

Jansson’s work on The Hobbit bears this out. Filled with dynamic movement and a sense of the sublime, it showcases a different side of her visual personality, even as its bears her unmistakable artistic

.

There is more than a hint of Snufkin (the free-spirited wanderer of her Moomin stories) about her Bilbo in his travelling cloak and out-sized hat. But the Misty Mountains are as far from Moominvalley as it’s possible to get, and the ruined gates of the Lonely Mountain

the monstrous jaws of Smaug the dragon himself, with plumes of billowing steam and dragon-fire.

Here and elsewhere, the characters are literally dwarfed by the landscapes they move through and the

they meet there. Consider Jansson’s Gollum. Far from a gnarled, shrunken hobbit, he towers over Bilbo like a slimy cave-troll. Those looking for illustrations that precisely match Tolkien’s words will find themselves disappointed. But I would argue that Jansson
the “ecstatic truth” of being a small person in a vast and imposing world – that is to say, of being a child.
